summary:
Adygea stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, same-sex marriage is prohibited, and no discrimination protection exists. The propaganda statutes and the extremist designation of the 'international LGBT movement' apply in Adygea as in every other Russian region, and foreigners who breach them face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols, of which 98 were administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges in connection with the designation, two of them sentenced to prison and seventeen pending or unknown. On 15 May 2025 three staff of two publishing houses were charged with running an extremist organisation under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years, and repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 assesses that lesbian, gay and bisexual people in Russia are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of sexual orientation, but that people in the North Caucasus, transgender people and those publicly active in LGBT+ advocacy are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. Adygea is not named as an exception to that assessment, so the note does not resolve whether the North Caucasus limb of the finding reaches this republic.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia covers general travel safety and includes the North Caucasus republics and interior-permission entry regimes among its stated concerns.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between the general baseline and the trans-specific finding is the central turbulence in the sources: the Home Office treats sexual orientation alone as insufficient for a persecution finding while treating gender identity, North Caucasus residence and public advocacy as sufficient, which means a trans visitor's exposure is assessed on different footing from that of a cisgender LGB traveller in the same location.

The Home Office note records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024, a figure that indicates enforcement volume alongside the conviction totals reported by Human Rights Watch.

Entry itself carries a separate layer of risk: the US State Department advisory flags interior-permission regimes, under which travel into certain areas requires prior authorisation, and the North Caucasus republics are named within the advisory's coverage.
localsOnly:
Residents of Adygea cannot obtain legal recognition of their gender, since gender transition on official documents has been banned nationwide since 2023, and gender-affirming healthcare is unavailable through lawful channels for the same period. Same-sex marriage is prohibited and no statutory discrimination protection covers gender identity or sexual orientation, so there is no domestic legal remedy for refusal of service, dismissal or mistreatment on those grounds.

Display of symbols associated with the designated 'international LGBT movement' exposes residents to administrative conviction, and repeated display is punishable by up to four years in prison. Charges under article 282.2 for running an extremist organisation carry up to 12 years, as the three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face.

Public LGBT+ advocacy is treated as an aggravating factor in the Home Office assessment, which finds that people publicly active in LGBT+ advocacy in Russia are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Adygea falls within the North Caucasus limb of the Home Office persecution finding is unresolved: the June 2025 note names the North Caucasus as a category and does not name Adygea as an exception, but it also does not enumerate the republics it includes. No Adygea-specific enforcement data, raid record or prosecution appears in the audited sources.

The Human Rights Watch breakdown of at least 20 criminal cases between January 2024 and June 2025 accounts for two sentences and seventeen pending or unknown outcomes, leaving the disposition of at least one case not sourced here.

The specific terms of the interior-permission entry regime referenced in the US State Department advisory, including whether Adygea requires a permit and on what basis, are not detailed in the available inventory and remain unverified.
